title: Fractions as Lengths
subtitle: Partitioned Fractions A
fit: Fits NSW Stage 2 Partitioned Fractions A (2 weeks)

outcomes.text: represents and compares halves, quarters, thirds and fifths as lengths on a number line and their related fractions formed by halving (eighths, sixths and tenths)

develops understanding and fluency in mathematics through exploring and connecting mathematical concepts, choosing and applying mathematical techniques to solve problems, and communicating their thinking and reasoning coherently and clearly

content: Make fractional parts of a length without relying on repeated halving
Make thirds and fifths of a length by estimating, checking and adjusting
Show unit fractions and count them to one complete whole on a number line
Use fraction strips and diagrams to model halves, quarters, eighths and thirds
Explain that fractions made from the same number of equal parts belong to one family with the same denominator
Find the part needed to complete one whole for halves, quarters, eighths and thirds
Rebuild the whole from a part (1/2, 1/4, 1/3, 1/8)
Compare unit fractions of the same whole as lengths

vocab.means: The full length we start with. A strip of 2 halves is still one whole, not 2 wholes.
Parts that are exactly the same length. Two pieces of 4 cm and 6 cm are not equal parts.
A number that tells us about equal parts of a whole. 3/4 means 3 parts when the whole has 4 equal parts.
The top number. It counts how many equal parts we are talking about. In 3/4 it is 3.
The bottom number. It tells how many equal parts make the whole. It is not how many parts are shaded.
A fraction with 1 on top, like 1/3 or 1/8. 2/3 is not a unit fraction.
A line where every number has its own place. We count the spaces from 0, not the marks.
Make a careful guess, check it, then move it a little until the parts are equal.
Fractions with the same denominator, like 1/8, 3/8 and 8/8. 3/8 and 3/4 are not in the same family.
The part you add to make exactly one whole. For 3/4 the missing part is 1/4, not 1/3.

misconceptions.think: 1/8 is bigger than 1/4 because 8 is bigger than 4.
misconceptions.fix: Fold two strips of the same length into quarters and eighths. Lay them side by side. More parts means each part is shorter.

misconceptions.think: To find 3/4 on a number line, count 3 marks, and 0 counts as the first one.
misconceptions.fix: Jump the spaces with a finger from 0. Say 'zero, one quarter, two quarters'. The number of spaces from 0 to 1 is the denominator.

misconceptions.think: Any 2 pieces are halves and any 3 pieces are thirds, even if they are different lengths.
misconceptions.fix: Check by laying parts on top of each other or measuring. Show near misses (9 cm, 10 cm, 11 cm) and ask if they are thirds.

misconceptions.think: Fractions stop at 1. You cannot have 5 quarters.
misconceptions.fix: Keep counting in quarters past 1 on a 0 to 2 number line. 4/4 lands on 1, so 5/4 is one quarter more.

misconceptions.think: 1/4 of my strip is longer than 1/2 of yours, so 1/4 is bigger than 1/2.
misconceptions.fix: Show that a fair comparison needs the same whole. Compare both fractions on one strip or two number lines of the same length.

signature.name: My Fraction Flip Book
signature.what: A strip-shaped flip book with one panel for each big idea; students add a strip, a number line and a sentence after each lesson.

panels.title: Halves
panels.prompt: Glue a folded strip. Mark 1/2 on a 0 to 1 number line. Finish: Halves are 2 ...

panels.title: Quarters and eighths
panels.prompt: Halve, then halve again. Label quarters and eighths on one line. Which part is shorter?

panels.title: Thirds and fifths
panels.prompt: Show how you made thirds and fifths by estimate and adjust. Write one tip for a friend.

panels.title: Count to one whole
panels.prompt: Count unit fractions to 1 on a number line. Write 1 whole three ways, like 4/4.

panels.title: Make one whole
panels.prompt: Draw a strip with a missing part. Write the number sentence, like 5/8 + 3/8 = 1.

panels.title: Rebuild the whole
panels.prompt: Glue one piece. Write its fraction. Draw the whole it came from and explain how you knew.

panels.title: Fraction families
panels.prompt: Pick a family. Write every member from the unit fraction to one whole.

panels.title: Compare unit fractions
panels.prompt: Order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 and 1/8. Finish: More parts means ...
